extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and typesetters (publishing professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: A publisher's manual of style covering manuscript preparation, spacing/indentation/heading conventions, proofs and make-up, and practical instructions for proofreaders and copyholders in book and journal production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abrupt line-spacing contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if at all avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid visually jarring alternation of leading between adjacent lines; aim for consistent spacing so the page reads smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hair-space or em-quad to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially adjust spacing by inserting hair-spaces or em-quads to force lines to fit; correct the composition instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line when an em indention available
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph that allows of an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer an indention rather than stretching the last line to fill measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal side spacing for short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like "a," "an," etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure visual consistency by giving small words balanced spacing on both sides; avoid visual lop-sidedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space after certain signs and before specific abbreviations/metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, f, and similar signs; before "f.," "ff.," and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: "§ 14. Be it further ordained . . . ."; use an appropriately small (thin) space rather than full word space around these marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency and unit spacing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols, $ and £ (pounds), 5. (shillings) and d. (pence), and the numerals: $2.75; £10  35.  2d.;  10°  C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard practice: place currency symbols adjacent to numerals without intervening space; follow other examples as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at line/center-head starts
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified quads to separate numerals from following text depending on context (subsection line vs center-head vs heading styles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture-reference spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus (use 9-unit colon): II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5 — 3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 9-unit colon spacing convention to set scripture citations consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between letters in products and before super/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: nx* = 2m2 (v2z2 — zvwyz -\-2W*y*). For mathematical/compositional expressions avoid added inter-letter spacing unless special typographic reasons require it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aligning figures in capitalized headings
rubrics_metrics.description: In capitalized headings use aligning figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lining (aligning) numerals in all-cap settings so numerals align visually with capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linotype composition indentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype composition in measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of from 10 to 20, indent X pt., 1 em; 10 pt., 11/2 em; 9 pt., 11/4 em; 8 pt., 11/4 em; 6 pt., 2 em. In measures of from 20 to 30, indent Y pt., 11/4 ems; 10 pt., 11/4; 9 pt., 11/4; 8 pt., 2; 6 pt., 2 1/4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric indention values are the recommended standard for plain paragraphs set on linotype; apply the appropriate indent based on measure and type size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype composition indentation alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: In monotype composition indentions should be such that all paragraph indentions align irrespective of the size of the type. Recommended indents for measures of 19 to 30 picas are given (e.g., N pt. indented 11/2 ems or 1 em 9 units; 10 pt. indented 11/2 ems or 1 em 12 units; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set indents so that paragraphs align across sizes; adjust proportionally for narrower or wider measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanging indention sizing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In hanging indentions, in measures of less than 10 picas, indent all sizes 1 em; from 10 to 20, N pt., 10 pt., 9 pt., and 8 pt., 11/2 ems; 6 pt., 2 ems; from 20 to 30, 11 pt., 10 pt., 9 pt., and 8 pt., 2 ems; 6 pt., 3 ems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed hanging indentation amounts by measure and point size when setting hanging paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; if the longest line is of disproportionate length strike an average of the long lines to give a centered appearance. Where quotations from different poems vary slightly in line length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines. In blank verse lines approximately same length should be aligned. If consecutive lines rhyme they should be aligned; if rhymes alternate indent the rhyming lines alike. Indent disproportionately short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the longest line (or an average of long lines) to determine centering; follow rhyme and line-length patterns to decide alignment/indention. Examples provided illustrate typical arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain paragraphs for ordinary reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable. Use hanging indention when desired to bring the opening word(s) into relief, or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to plain (first-line indented) paragraphs for readability; reserve hanging indents for emphasis or long center-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard lead and slug definitions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary standard lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without, solid. A slug is a strip of metal thicker than a lead; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standard sizes to control interline spacing and to insert spacing after headlines, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins; usually set in caps or small caps, and not followed by a period. When a center-head makes more than one line, either the (inverted) 'pyramid' form (for two or three lines) or 'hanging indention' (for more than three lines) is employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set center-heads in appropriate caps and arrange multi-line center-heads in pyramid or hanging indention forms as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column; it may be set in a separate line flush with the margin or run in as a continuous line with the paragraph. Side-heads are most frequently set in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized; sometimes in caps & small caps or bold face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the side-head form (flush separate line or run-in) based on design; prefer italics with sentence-style capitalization unless a different style is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in head and box-head definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type and placed under the first two lines of the paragraph. A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cut-in or box-heads for special side treatments; set in contrasting type and position as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-head conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page, usually giving the main title on the verso and the chapter or subdivision title on the recto. It should be centered regardless of page number. A good working rule is to set running-heads in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than the type of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure running-heads are consistent, centered, and two sizes smaller than body text; place main title left, chapter title right as standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph kinds: plain vs hanging
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of paragraphs are distinguished — plain (regular) and hanging. A plain paragraph has the first line indented and the others set flush. A hanging paragraph has the first line set flush and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the defined formats correctly and consistently in manuscript and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of proofs and their usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Galley-proof is a printed impression of type in a galley; page-proof is impression made up into page-form; plate-proof or foundry-proof is a proof taken immediately before an electrotype cast (has a black border); foul proof is a galley-proof containing author's corrections; a revise is a new proof corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and handle proofs by their types; be aware plate-proofs differ visually (black border) and most publications are printed from plates today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up, folio, half-title and submission of special copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up is arranging into page-form of type-lines and illustrations. A folio is a page-number (even on verso, odd on recto). A half-title or bastard title is abbreviated title placed on a separate page preceding the full title-page or part/chapter. Copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables of contents, etc., should be submitted with the manuscript. Copy for indexes should be compiled from the special set of page-proofs furnished for this purpose and promptly delivered to the printers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply required special copy with manuscript in timely fashion to avoid unnecessary delay in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation: presentation and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be either typewritten or in a perfectly clear handwriting (typewritten preferable). Sheets should be of uniform size (9"x11" desirable), use only one side, never roll manuscripts, place flat in a box or envelope, and sheets should not be fastened together except by pins or clips which can be easily removed. When one piece of a page is fastened to another, use mucilage, not pins. Liberal margins should be left at the top and left-hand side for directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these physical presentation rules to facilitate accurate copy-holding, proofing, and typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbering and marking inserts/omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., sheets to be inserted after p. 4 marked '4A', '4B', etc.; sheets omitted between p. 4 and p. 8 indicated by numbering p. 4, '4–7'). Additions to original pages should be placed after the sheets to which they belong and marked 'Insert A,' 'Insert B,' etc., and places where they are to be inserted indicated by writing 'Here insert A' on the margin of the original pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number and label all changes and insertions clearly to avoid misplacement and resetting errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a ¶ mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make paragraph breaks explicit to assist copyholders and proofreaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote conventions and numbering practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes should be clearly designated, either by separating them from the text by running a line across the page or by using ink of different color. The word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts. Number them consecutively throughout an article or by chapters in a book, bearing in mind that in linotype composition changes of a number may necessitate resetting many lines; monotype or hand-set matter does not have that difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer consecutive numbering through article/chapters but be aware of linotype resetting costs; mark footnotes clearly and never embed them inline in manuscript body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names and foreign words legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names, foreign words, and figures should, in handwritten manuscript, be written with the utmost care and distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illegible names/foreign words cause misprints — take care to make them unmistakable in manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and returning proofs promptly; use standard marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets use the standard proofreaders' marks. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs. Remember that changes in the type cost money; make your manuscript as perfect as possible before delivering it to the printer. Any necessary alterations should be made in the galley-proof; corrections in plates should be studiously avoided. The original manuscript should be returned with the galley-proof, and each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness, use of standard marks, answering queries, limiting late changes, and providing prior marked sets are essential to control cost and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreader professional responsibilities and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures and verify all dates. If copy is not clear or you doubt correctness, look it up or query the author. Make queries clear and transfer queries made in the manuscript to the proof. Be discreet about queries—do not ask foolish questions—and do not stultify yourself or discredit the office. Make a study of the 'personal equation' of editors/authors. Never hesitate to correct anything palpably wrong, even if copy asserts the contrary. Do not follow copy blindly; follow only when correct. Do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style—the Manual is meant for you. Do not assume an author's O.K. relieves you of responsibility. Do not shield behind the copyholder; investigate if in doubt. Do not read to the copyholder except in special cases. Cultivate speed but remember accuracy is more important. In unavoidable rushes protect yourself by disclaiming further responsibility if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are core professional duties and attitudes for proofreaders: exercise judgment, verify facts, be discreet, prioritize accuracy, and accept responsibility for typographic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading workflow, records and handling of proof sets
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing reading, sign all galley-proofs and page-proofs in the upper right-hand corner with your initial above that of the copyholder and reviser. Mark number of proofs wanted on first readings. Return all proofs ready to be corrected to the desk. When galley-proofs are ready to go out, give the copy to the file clerk in perfect order, with proofs neatly arranged in required sets pinned at the top. When reading page-proofs, revise by checking with author's alterations first, next make copy for contents and return to be set so cover and contents may be ready with page-proofs. Record number of pages and plates and total pages in the finished product including preliminaries. See that the finished book or journal will contain even forms of 16, 12, or 8 pages; raise the question if not. Number and indicate half-titles, blank pages, inserts, etc., and carry all necessary queries on every set of proofs. When pages are ready, place them neatly in sets pinned at the top and return to the file clerk with all galley-proofs and additional copy in order of make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear physical organization, sign-offs, and make-up records to enable correct charging and timely production; attend to pagination/form counts required for printing imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder practice and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading voice. Small words are as essential as big ones — get them all in right. Enunciate plural 's' distinctly. Regulate and equalize speed; do not race through typewritten copy while fumbling with manuscript. Do not keep guessing at a word—look closely and consider context. Give the proofreader a chance to make corrections; slow up when the proofreader puts pencil to paper. Evolve a private system of signals to indicate special treatments. Read every instruction, editorial mark and stet-mark carefully. Learn the job number and read it for every galley. Consult job ticket for number of proofs and recipient address before having proofs corrected. Be careful in transferring marks; a mark in the wrong place means two errors uncorrected. Ensure everything is present when sending out proofs; arrange copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. The manuscript should accompany galley-proof; the foul proof should accompany the page-proof. Indicate envelope contents in lower left-hand corner; fasten pins at center top not diagonally. Return reference volumes and proofs to file daily. Keep the proof-room neat and orderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyholders must read clearly, manage marks precisely, follow job tickets, and maintain housekeeping so proofs move through the process without error or delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard proofreader's marks
rubrics_metrics.description: In marking proofs use the standard proofreaders' marks (examples follow): dele (delete); letter reversed (turn); put in space; close up (no space); bad spacing — space more/less/evenly; wrong font/character of wrong size or style; transpose; make a new paragraph; indent or put in an em-quad space; carry left/right; imperfect type — correct; space shows between words — push down; straighten crooked line; straighten alignment; restore certain words crossed out; print as ligature; words are omitted; query to author; put in capitals; put in small capitals; put in lower case; put in italic type; put in bold face; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and use the conventional marks rather than inventing idiosyncratic symbols; a provided list and exemplars should be followed to ensure compositor comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid late and expensive corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in the type cost money. The omission or addition of a word in the middle of a paragraph may necessitate resetting the whole of this from that point on; if such alteration is made in the page-proof, it may further involve repaging the entire article or chapter. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided. Not only are they expensive, but they are likely to injure the plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make manuscripts as perfect as possible before delivering to the printer and confine changes to earlier proof stages to limit cost and damage.
